study.title: Judges 14 - Samson, the riddle and the beginning of the conflict with the Philistines
study.overview: This chapter shows Samson acting under the sovereign direction of God, though strangely and morally unstable. He desires to marry a Philistine woman, defeat a lion with the strength of the Spirit of the LORD, finds honey within the dead animal, proposes a riddle at his wedding banquet, is betrayed by the pressure of his wife and, in the end, reacts with anger against the Philistines. The text presents both the human weakness of Samson and the divine purpose of seeking occasion against the Philistines, who dominated Israel at that time.

outline.title: The Choice of Samson and God's Purpose
outline.explanation: Samson descends to Timna, sees a Philistine woman and insists on taking her for a wife, despite her parents' resistance. The narrator explains that this came from the LORD, who sought occasion against the Philistines. The chapter already introduces the tension between personal desire, limits of the covenant and God's government on history.

outline.title: The expired lion and honey in the corpse
outline.explanation: On the way to Timna, Samson faces a young lion, and the Spirit of the Lord enables him to shatter him without weapons. Later, upon returning, he finds bees and honey in the body of the lion, eats him and also offers to his parents, without revealing the origin. The episode shows supernatural power, but also secret and ambiguity.

outline.title: The banquet, the puzzle and the betrayal
outline.explanation: Samson performs the custom of the wedding banquet and receives thirty companions. He proposes a lion-based puzzle and honey; men cannot solve and turn to Samson's wife with threat and pressure. After seven days of insistent crying, she convinces him to reveal the answer, and the Philistines triumph with the solution before sunset.

outline.title: The wrath of Samson and the breakup of the wedding
outline.explanation: The Spirit of the LORD returns to act on Samson, who goes to Askelon, kills thirty men and takes his spoils to pay the bet. Taken from anger, he returns to his father's house, and the woman is given to the companion accompanying him. Marriage quickly undoes, and the conflict with the Philistines intensifies.

study.context: The notes indicate that Timna was a border town of the Philistines, linked to the territory of Judah and later attributed to Dan. They also note that marriage to a woman outside the people of Israel contradicted the law, according to the texts cited in the notes. The chapter explicitly states that the Philistines dominated Israel in that period, which helps to understand the background of oppression and confrontation.
study.theology: The chapter highlights God's sovereignty by acting through confusing human decisions. Samson is not presented as a simple moral model, but as an instrument of divine providence to begin confrontation with the Philistines. The expression of the Spirit of the LORD teaches that Samson's victory does not proceed primarily from natural capacity, but from divine empowerment. At the same time, the text shows the dangers of the guided desire only by what pleases the eyes, lack of transparency and manipulation within relationships. There is also a contrast between force and vulnerability: Samson wins a lion, but is entangled by human pressures and ends in anger and loss. The text does not automatically approve your choices; rather, it shows that God acts despite them to fulfill his purpose.

scholarViews.insight: Samson appears as a strange instrument of providence: God uses even his marriage to a Philistine to seek occasion against the Philistines, showing that he is not presented as a standard to be imitated, but as a figure of a greater purpose of God.
The expression of Samson descending to Timna is understood as a reference to a border town of the Philistines, located on the border of the territory connected to Judah and then attributed to Dan.

questions: What does the text teach about the difference between what pleases the eyes and what is in accordance with the will of God?
How does the performance of the Spirit of the Lord in Samson guide our understanding of God's strength, vocation and dependence?
What spiritual dangers appear in the way Samson deals with secret, alliances, and pressure within marriage?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a warning against guided decisions only by immediate desire. Examine whether your choices have been shaped by what seems pleasing at the moment or by fidelity to God. The chapter also calls to trust that God remains sovereign even in confusing scenarios, but without using it as an excuse for moral recklessness. In practice, it is worth cultivating transparency, discernment and submission to the Lord in relationships, remembering that spiritual strength does not replace obedience.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not detail all the historical aspects of Timna, nor do they explain in depth the chronology of the Philistine domain. Nor do they allow to affirm with certainty to what extent Samson consciously understood the divine purpose behind his actions. Adam Clarke's interpretation of the phrase 'this came from the Lord' as divine permission is an interpretative reading, not an explicit definition of the text.
